hinjewadi.text: Hinjewadi is home to the Rajiv Gandhi Infotech Park, a 2,800-acre technology and business park built by MIDC that hosts offices of over 800 companies. In September 2026 the Pune district collector said more than five lakh people travel to and from Hinjawadi every day.

hinjewadi.text: New housing in Hinjewadi includes large high-rise apartment projects; in October 2025 Shriram Properties signed a joint development agreement for a roughly 0.7 million sq ft high-rise mixed-use residential project there. hinjewadi.text: Much of the residential development in the Hinjewadi–Maan–Marunji area is recent: August 2026 reports describe rapid urbanisation and a sharp rise in the IT industry and population over the past few years. Residents say roads, water supply and other civic infrastructure have not kept pace with this growth.

hinjewadi.text: Hinjewadi is not inside a municipal corporation: civic responsibilities are split between MIDC, PMRDA and local gram panchayats, with the Zilla Parishad and the state PWD also active in the IT park area. A proposal to merge Hinjewadi, Maan, Marunji and four other villages into the Pimpri Chinchwad Municipal Corporation, approved by the PCMC general body in 2015, got a fresh push from the Chief Minister in September 2026 but had not been finalised at the time of that report.

sources.title: Pune: Hinjewadi Merger With PCMC Gets Fresh Push, CM Fadnavis Says Decision Soon
sources.quote: Hinjewadi, which houses a major IT hub employing a large number of people, has for years faced infrastructure and civic issues amid fragmented jurisdiction involving the Maharashtra Industrial Development Corporation (MIDC), Pune Metropolitan Region Development Authority (PMRDA) and local gram panchayats.

sources.title: Pune: PMRDA Throws Up Hands Ahead Of Monsoon, Says ‘Don’t Blame Us Alone If Hinjawadi Floods Again’
sources.quote: Speaking to the press recently, Dr Chaudhari explained that multiple government agencies like PMRDA, Maharashtra Industrial Development Corporation (MIDC), local Gram Panchayats, Pune Zilla Parishad, and the state’s Public Works Department (PWD) operate in the Hinjawadi IT Park area.

hinjewadi.text: In its jurisdiction, which covers parts of the Hinjawadi area, PMRDA requires developers to obtain a groundwater availability certificate from the Groundwater Surveys and Development Agency before it approves new building proposals or occupancy certificates; in August 2026 this was reported to be delaying approvals by up to two months. Hinjawadi–Maan–Marunji residents have also demanded that PMRDA stop granting new construction and housing permissions until water is assured for existing societies.

sources.title: Pune: PMRDA's Mandatory Groundwater Certificate Delays Building Approvals by Up to Two Months
sources.quote: The Pune Metropolitan Region Development Authority (PMRDA) has made it mandatory for developers to obtain a groundwater availability certificate from the Groundwater Surveys and Development Agency (GSDA) while seeking approval for new building proposals and occupancy certificates.

sources.title: Pune: PMRDA Throws Up Hands Ahead Of Monsoon, Says ‘Don’t Blame Us Alone If Hinjawadi Floods Again’
sources.quote: Some parts of Hinjawadi IT Park fall under the authority.

hinjewadi.text: Housing societies near the Hinjewadi IT parks have long depended on private water tankers; a 2018 report said they had to rely completely on tankers while adjoining villages received piped water every two days for 20 minutes. In June 2026 a Maharashtra Jeevan Pradhikaran water supply scheme for Hinjawadi's IT companies was reported stalled because its water quota had not been sanctioned, while PMRDA sought 1.2 TMC from Mulshi Dam for a permanent supply.

sources.quote: However, work on the scheme has remained stalled as the water quota has not yet been sanctioned.

hinjewadi.text: Roads in the Hinjawadi IT Park flood during intense monsoon bursts: on 7 June 2025 a downpour of only a few minutes submerged parts of Telco Road and Landewadi, and heavy waterlogging recurred on 22 June 2025. The flooding was traced to natural streams and nullahs blocked by encroachments and to a failed drainage system.
